title: The Loves of the Boy and Girl at School

keywords: the loves of the boy and girl at school
full_text:
In an ancient quarter of Baghdad stood a famous school where children of noble families were instructed in the Quran, Arabic grammar, the art of calligraphy, and the composition of classical poetry.

Among the pupils was a handsome boy named Qasim, son of a respected merchant, and a bright, graceful girl named Jamila, daughter of the Chief Scribe. Both excelled above all their companions in quickness of intellect and beauty of penmanship. While the other children struggled with ink-horns and reed pens, Qasim and Jamila composed spontaneous verses upon their polished wooden slates, passing them across the wooden benches with quiet smiles.

One morning, the strict schoolmaster noticed Qasim inscribing a poetic verse upon his slate instead of copying the day's grammar lesson:
'The ink upon this wooden slate shall fade with time away,
Yet honor, truth, and faithful hearts forever live and stay.'

The schoolmaster picked up Jamila's slate, and found that she had written in response:
'Like rivers flowing toward the sea that never part their course,
The soul that seeks the highest good drinks from an endless source.'

The master frowned, tapped his cane upon his desk, and declared: 'School is an academy of serious learning, not an exchange for poets!' He threatened to summon their parents and chastise them with his palm-switch.

However, the Chief Scribe happened to enter the classroom at that moment to inspect his daughter's progress. Reading the two slates, the scribe was struck by the moral maturity, elegance of meter, and exquisite calligraphy of the children.

'Hold your cane, master!' said the scribe with a proud smile. 'These two children have mastered grammar, meter, and virtue before their years! An affection founded upon mutual reverence for wisdom is a flower to be nurtured, not crushed.'

The families agreed that when the children attained maturity, their union should be celebrated. Years later, Qasim became a celebrated statesman and Jamila a renowned scholar, their lifelong companionship having sprouted from two polished wooden slates.
moral: Innocent affection, refined learning, and mutual respect in youth lay the foundation for enduring character.
